pos: v. (disowned; cast off publicly; refused to have to do with)
etymology: Greek apeipomen, to speak off or speak away from oneself — to disown by declaration. The English comes through French renoncer, from Latin renuntiare, to announce back, to disclaim formally.
biblical_def: But have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God. Paul is describing the integrity of a gospel ministry, and he begins with a renunciation. The word is decisive: not resisted, not struggled against, but renounced — formally disowned, put away by a settled act. What is renounced is named in three parts, and all three concern method rather than message. The hidden things of dishonesty are the concealed practices a man would not want examined. Craftiness is the readiness to manage people. And handling the word of God deceitfully is the adulteration of the text itself — trimming it, weighting it, using it to get a result it does not warrant. Against all three Paul sets one method: by manifestation of the truth. The truth is simply set out in the open, and it commends itself to the conscience. This is the apostolic pattern and the church's permanent standard: we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord. A ministry that must manage its hearers to hold them has already abandoned the only instrument God has promised to bless.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to disown; to disclaim; to reject; to cast off, as a connection; to declare against.
webster_full: RENOUNCE, v.t. To disown; to disclaim; to reject; as, to renounce a title or a claim.
RENOUNCE, v.t. To deny; to cast off; to reject; to disclaim; as, to renounce allegiance.
RENOUNCED, pp. Disowned; denied; rejected; disclaimed.
DISHONESTY, n. Want of probity or integrity in principle; faithlessness; a disposition to defraud, deceive or betray.
CRAFTINESS, n. Cunning; artifice; stratagem; dexterity in devising and effecting a purpose.
scriptures: 2 Corinthians 4:2

But have renounced the hidden things of dishonesty, not walking in craftiness, nor handling the word of God deceitfully; but by manifestation of the truth commending ourselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God.
2 Corinthians 4:1
Therefore seeing we have this ministry, as we have received mercy, we faint not;
2 Corinthians 4:5
For we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord; and ourselves your servants for Jesus' sake.
2 Corinthians 4:7
But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us.
corruption_summary: Ministry method has been widely detached from ministry message, so that technique borrowed from marketing is held to be neutral; Paul renounces the management of hearers as a thing incompatible with the gospel itself.
corruption_paragraphs: The governing assumption of much church practice is that the message is fixed while the methods are free — that whatever gathers a crowd may be used, since the content preached to the crowd is sound. 2 Corinthians 4:2 denies the premise. Paul renounces craftiness as such, and he does so in the same sentence in which he describes his preaching, because for him the two cannot be separated. A gospel that is true commends itself by manifestation of the truth, plainly set out. Where a ministry depends on managing impressions, the method has already begun to preach a different message than the words do.

The subtler form is the deceitful handling of the word itself, which rarely announces itself as dishonesty. It is the text pressed past what it says to secure a response; the verse lifted from its argument because it moves an audience; the hard clause quietly left out. Every such adjustment is made for a good end, which is exactly why Paul had to renounce it rather than merely avoid it. The remedy he names is not more sincerity but more exposure — truth manifested, in the sight of God, to the conscience, where no technique reaches and none is needed.
roots_summary: Greek apeipomen (G550), to disown or renounce; panourgia (G3834), craftiness; doloo (G1389), to adulterate or handle deceitfully; phanerosis (G5321), manifestation.
roots_lines: Greek apeipomen (G550) — to speak away from oneself, to disown formally; rendered renounced, its only occurrence.
Greek panourgia (G3834) — unscrupulous cleverness, readiness for anything; rendered craftiness.
Greek doloo (G1389) — to adulterate, as a merchant dilutes wine; rendered handling deceitfully.
Greek phanerosis (G5321) — a making manifest, an uncovering; the apostolic method, set against all three renunciations.
Greek suneidesis (G4893) — conscience; the faculty to which manifested truth commends itself.
usage: “renounced the hidden things of dishonesty” — a settled disowning, not a struggle.
“nor handling the word of God deceitfully” — the adulteration of the text.
“by manifestation of the truth” — the only method named.

pos: v. (to flow back; to overflow toward; to result in)
etymology: Latin redundare, to overflow, from re-, back, and unda, a wave. The Authorized Version uses it once, to render the Greek perisseuo, to abound — grace overflowing and returning as thanksgiving.
biblical_def: For all things are for your sakes, that the abundant grace might through the thanksgiving of many redound to the glory of God. The word carries a wave rolling back, and the whole verse is a circuit. Grace goes out from God, abundantly; it is received by many; it returns to God as thanksgiving; and the returning wave is glory. Paul states the purpose of his own afflictions this way, and the logic is worth following closely, because it reverses the ordinary account of suffering. All things are for your sakes — the hardship of the ministry is not incidental but instrumental, aimed at the church's good. But the church's good is not the terminus either. The grace that reaches them is meant to travel further, and it travels by way of their thanksgiving, arriving at last where everything in Scripture arrives, at the glory of God. Two things follow. Thanksgiving is not a courtesy appended to grace received; it is the appointed channel by which grace completes its circuit. And the more grace abounds in the many, the greater the glory returned — which is precisely why God is able to make all grace abound toward you. The believer's gratitude is not decoration on the doctrine of grace. It is the doctrine finishing its work.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): to be sent, driven or rolled back; to conduce in the consequence; to contribute; to result.
webster_full: REDOUND, v.i. To be sent, driven or rolled back; to roll back, as a wave.
REDOUND, v.i. To conduce in the consequence; to contribute; to result; as, our conduct may redound to our honor.
REDOUND, v.i. To proceed in the consequence or effect; to result.
THANKSGIVING, n. The act of rendering thanks or expressing gratitude for favors or mercies.
ABUNDANT, a. Plentiful; in great quantity; fully sufficient; as an abundant supply.
scriptures: 2 Corinthians 4:15
For all things are for your sakes, that the abundant grace might through the thanksgiving of many redound to the glory of God.
2 Corinthians 9:8
And God is able to make all grace abound toward you; that ye, always having all sufficiency in all things, may abound to every good work:
2 Corinthians 1:11
Ye also helping together by prayer for us, that for the gift bestowed upon us by the means of many persons thanks may be given by many on our behalf.
1 Corinthians 10:31
Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God.
corruption_summary: Grace is commonly presented as terminating in the believer's benefit; Paul makes the believer a station on a circuit whose destination is the glory of God.
corruption_paragraphs: Where the gospel is preached chiefly as a remedy for the hearer's felt needs, grace is made to stop at the point of relief, and thanksgiving becomes an optional response for those so inclined. 2 Corinthians 4:15 will not allow the circuit to be broken there. The abundant grace is given that it might redound to the glory of God, and the purpose clause governs the whole. A doctrine of grace that ends in the recipient has not merely underemphasized God's glory; it has stopped the wave halfway and lost the reason the grace was given.

The second distortion is more pious in appearance and appears wherever affliction is explained solely by what it produces in the sufferer. Paul does say all things are for the church's sake, and the dictionary does not diminish it. But he keeps going. The sufferings of the ministry serve the saints, the saints give thanks, and the thanks return as glory to God. To halt the sentence at the middle term is to make the Christian the end of God's dealings, which is the very inversion that idolatry makes. The comfort in the doctrine is real, and it is greater when the circuit is left whole: a believer's worst season is already enlisted in the return of glory to God.
roots_summary: Greek perisseuo (G4052), to abound or overflow; eucharistia (G2169), thanksgiving; charis (G5485), grace; doxa (G1391), glory.
roots_lines: Greek perisseuo (G4052) — to superabound, to overflow; rendered redound here and abound elsewhere.
Greek eucharistia (G2169) — thanksgiving; the channel by which the grace returns.
Greek charis (G5485) — grace, free favour; described here as abundant.
Greek doxa (G1391) — glory; the destination of the circuit.
Greek pleonazo (G4121) — to make to abound, to multiply; joined to perisseuo in Paul's vocabulary of overflowing grace.
usage: “redound to the glory of God” — the wave returning to its source.
“through the thanksgiving of many” — the appointed channel of return.
“all things are for your sakes” — the middle term, not the last.

pos: adj. (whole in every part; complete; with nothing missing)
etymology: Greek holokleros, from holos, whole, and kleros, a lot or portion — having every part that belongs to it, with no portion lacking. The word was used of a sacrificial animal without defect and of a body with all its limbs sound.
biblical_def: But let patience have her perfect work, that ye may be perfect and entire, wanting nothing. James is writing about trials, and this is the purpose he assigns them. The two adjectives are not synonyms. Perfect (teleios) is a word of maturity — having reached the end for which a thing was made. Entire (holokleros) is a word of wholeness — having every part, with nothing absent. A man may be mature in one region of his character and missing a portion in another; James says the finished work leaves neither deficiency. And he makes patience the instrument. The trying of your faith worketh patience, and patience is to be given her perfect work, which means the believer is not to cut the process short. That is the practical burden of the verse. Trials are not merely endured until they pass; they are the means by which the parts that are missing are supplied. The command count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations is therefore not a demand for cheerfulness under pain but a judgment about what the pain is doing. And the promise stands at the end of the same argument: blessed is the man that endureth temptation: for when he is tried, he shall receive the crown of life.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): whole; undivided; unbroken; complete in its parts; full; perfect; not deficient.
webster_full: ENTIRE, a. Whole; undivided; unbroken; complete in its parts.
ENTIRE, a. Full; complete; comprehending all requisites in itself.
ENTIRE, a. Sincere; unfeigned; in full strength; unmingled.
PATIENCE, n. The suffering of afflictions, pain, toil, calamity, provocation or other evil, with a calm, unruffled temper; endurance without murmuring or fretfulness.
PERFECT, a. Finished; complete; consummate; not defective; having all that is requisite to its nature and kind.
scriptures: James 1:4
But let patience have her perfect work, that ye may be perfect and entire, wanting nothing.
James 1:2
My brethren, count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations;
James 1:3
Knowing this, that the trying of your faith worketh patience.
James 1:12
Blessed is the man that endureth temptation: for when he is tried, he shall receive the crown of life, which the Lord hath promised to them that love him.
corruption_summary: The passage is read either as a promise of sinless perfection in this life or as mere encouragement to cope; James teaches a real and progressive completeness wrought by God through trials and not yet finished.
corruption_paragraphs: Perfectionist readings take perfect and entire, wanting nothing as a state attainable now, and every such scheme — from the medieval counsels through the higher-life movements — founders on the same rock: the believer who claims it must either redefine sin downward or deceive himself, and the apostle John forecloses both. James himself writes a few lines later that in many things we offend all. The completeness in view is the whole man being supplied in every part as patience does her work, a work still in progress in every living Christian. Sanctification is progressive, and its finish is glorification.

The therapeutic reading flattens the verse in the other direction, treating trials as occasions for resilience and the promised wholeness as a settled inner equilibrium. That empties the text of God. James does not say hardship builds character; he says the trying of your faith worketh patience, and he ends with the crown of life promised to them that love him. The difference is the difference between a believer who is being made whole by his God and a man managing his own adversity. Only one of them can count it all joy, and only because he knows who is doing the work and what it is for.
roots_summary: Greek holokleros (G3648), complete in every part; teleios (G5046), mature, finished; hupomone (G5281), patient endurance; dokimion (G1383), the trying or proving.
roots_lines: Greek holokleros (G3648) — whole in every portion, with nothing lacking; rendered entire.
Greek teleios (G5046) — brought to its end, mature; rendered perfect, and not meaning sinless.
Greek hupomone (G5281) — a remaining under, patient endurance; rendered patience.
Greek dokimion (G1383) — the proving of metal by fire; rendered the trying of your faith.
Greek leipo (G3007) — to lack, to be destitute; rendered wanting nothing, and again of wisdom in the next verse.
usage: “perfect and entire, wanting nothing” — mature, and whole in every part.
“let patience have her perfect work” — the process not to be cut short.
“the trying of your faith worketh patience” — the instrument named.

etymology: Greek artigennetos, from arti, just now, and gennao, to beget or bring forth — just-born. The compound occurs once in the New Testament, and it is a figure for believers, not for infants.
biblical_def: As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby. Peter has just said what makes the figure fit: being born again, not of corruptible seed, but of incorruptible, by the word of God, which liveth and abideth for ever. Because regeneration is a real birth, the newly regenerate are really newborn, and the appetite proper to a newborn is the one Peter commands. The comparison presses at three points. A newborn's hunger is instinctive and urgent, not cultivated. It is undiscriminating about everything except its object — milk, and nothing else will do. And it is aimed at growth, which is the reason the appetite exists. Sincere here means unadulterated, unmixed, without additive; the same concern Paul shows when he refuses to handle the word of God deceitfully. Peter is commanding a desire for the word itself, undiluted, and giving the reason plainly: that ye may grow thereby. The verse also settles a question about the Christian life at its start. The new birth is God's work, not the believer's — except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God. But the growth that follows comes by an appointed food, and the newborn is commanded to want it. The next verse gives the ground of the appetite: if so be ye have tasted that the Lord is gracious.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): recently born; as a newborn infant. NEW, lately made, invented, produced or come into being.
webster_full: NEWBORN, a. Recently born; as a newborn infant.
NEW, a. Lately made, invented, produced, or come into being; that has existed a short time only.
BABE, n. An infant; a young child of either sex.
SINCERE, a. Pure; unmixed; unadulterated; as sincere milk; sincere doctrine.
MILK, n. A white fluid secreted for the nourishment of the young; figuratively, the first and plainest doctrine.
scriptures: 1 Peter 2:2
As newborn babes, desire the sincere milk of the word, that ye may grow thereby:
1 Peter 1:23
Being born again, not of corruptible seed, but of incorruptible, by the word of God, which liveth and abideth for ever.
John 3:3
Jesus answered and said unto him, Verily, verily, I say unto thee, Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.
1 Peter 2:3
If so be ye have tasted that the Lord is gracious.
corruption_summary: The new birth is widely reduced to a decision the sinner makes, and the milk of the word to whatever a reader finds edifying; Peter makes regeneration God's act by his word and the milk the unadulterated word itself.
corruption_paragraphs: Where regeneration is treated as the sinner's own decision, the figure of a newborn collapses, because no infant begets itself. Peter is explicit about the agency and the instrument: born again, not of corruptible seed, but of incorruptible, by the word of God. The Reformed doctrine of the effectual call is not an imposition on these texts; it is what they say. The Lord told Nicodemus that a man must be born again to see the kingdom at all, which places the new birth before sight, not after choice. A gospel invitation is rightly pressed on every hearer, and the dictionary presses it; but the life that answers is given, not generated.

The second corruption is gentler and nearly universal: the sincere milk of the word read as any spiritual nourishment a believer happens to find sustaining — a devotional, a conference, a moving song. Sincere means unmixed, and the genitive is of the word. Peter is not commending an appetite for religious material; he is commanding hunger for Scripture itself, unadulterated. A church that substitutes commentary on the word for the word has quietly weaned its newborns, and the growth Peter promises comes only thereby.
roots_summary: Greek artigennetos (G738), newborn; anagennao (G313), to beget again; adolos (G97), without guile or adulteration; logikos (G3050), of the word.
roots_lines: Greek artigennetos (G738) — just-born; rendered newborn, its only occurrence.
Greek anagennao (G313) — to beget again; used by Peter alone, of God begetting his people.
Greek adolos (G97) — unadulterated, without guile; rendered sincere, the negative of doloo, to adulterate.
Greek logikos (G3050) — of the word, rational; the milk is the word's own.
Greek auxano (G837) — to grow; the purpose for which the appetite is commanded.
usage: “as newborn babes” — the figure follows the fact of regeneration.
“the sincere milk of the word” — unmixed, with no additive.
“that ye may grow thereby” — the appointed means of growth.

pos: n. pl. (suspicions; conjectures formed without evidence)
etymology: Greek huponoia, an under-thought — a suspicion formed beneath the surface of what is actually known. The English comes through Old French surmise, from Latin supermittere, to send or put upon; and so, to lay a charge upon by conjecture.
biblical_def: He is proud, knowing nothing, but doting about questions and strifes of words, whereof cometh envy, strife, railings, evil surmisings. Paul is describing a particular kind of man in the church and tracing what he produces. The portrait begins with a diagnosis that pairs two things the world would not pair: proud, knowing nothing. The pride is not the fruit of learning but the substitute for it. What such a man does have is an appetite — doting about questions and strifes of words, a sickly craving for dispute over terms. And Paul lists the harvest: envy, strife, railings, evil surmisings. The last of the four is the quietest and the most corrosive. A surmising is an under-thought, a suspicion about a brother's motive that runs beneath what is actually known and is never brought into the open where it could be tested. It requires no evidence, answers to no correction, and spreads without ever being stated outright. Paul calls these surmisings evil, which settles the question of whether a thought entertained privately about another man is a morally neutral thing. It is not. James forbids the practice at its root: speak not evil one of another, brethren. And Paul's counsel about the man who generates such things is blunt: from such withdraw thyself.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): suspicion; the thought or imagination that something may be, of which there is no proof or certain knowledge.
webster_full: SURMISE, n. A suspicion; the thought or imagination that something may be, of which, however, there is no certain or strong evidence.
SURMISE, v.t. To suspect; to imagine without certain knowledge; to entertain thoughts that something does or may exist.
SURMISING, ppr. Suspecting; imagining upon slight evidence.
RAILING, n. Reproachful or insolent language; clamorous abuse.
ENVY, n. Pain, uneasiness, mortification or discontent excited by the sight of another's superiority or success.
scriptures: 1 Timothy 6:4
He is proud, knowing nothing, but doting about questions and strifes of words, whereof cometh envy, strife, railings, evil surmisings,
1 Timothy 6:5
Perverse disputings of men of corrupt minds, and destitute of the truth, supposing that gain is godliness: from such withdraw thyself.
James 4:11

Speak not evil one of another, brethren. He that speaketh evil of his brother, and judgeth his brother, speaketh evil of the law, and judgeth the law: but if thou judge the law, thou art not a doer of the law, but a judge.
Galatians 5:15
But if ye bite and devour one another, take heed that ye be not consumed one of another.
corruption_summary: Suspicion of motive is now treated as discernment and even as a duty, so that the sin Paul names is practised under the character of vigilance.
corruption_paragraphs: The habit of reading motives has acquired a good name. To attribute an unstated interest to a brother — ambition, cowardice, self-protection — is presented as insight into what is really going on, and a Christian who declines to do it is thought naive. Paul files the practice under sin and calls it evil surmisings. The reason is plain enough: a surmising cannot be answered. A stated charge can be examined and either proved or dropped, which is why Scripture requires two or three witnesses; an under-thought about a man's heart escapes that discipline entirely while doing the damage of an accusation. Genuine discernment tests doctrine and conduct, both of which are public. It does not pronounce on motives it cannot see.

The online form of this sin deserves naming, since it is where most Christians now practise it. A congregation that would not permit an unsubstantiated charge from the floor of a members' meeting will pass one along in a thread without a second thought, and the speed of the medium supplies the appearance of consensus that the evidence never supplied. Paul's list runs envy, strife, railings, surmisings, and they travel together because they feed one another. His remedy is not better argument but distance: from such withdraw thyself.
roots_summary: Greek huponoia (G5283), a suspicion or under-thought; poneros (G4190), evil; logomachia (G3055), strife about words; phthonos (G5355), envy.
roots_lines: Greek huponoia (G5283) — an under-thought, a surmise; rendered surmisings, its only occurrence.
Greek poneros (G4190) — evil, malignant; the adjective Paul attaches, settling the moral question.
Greek logomachia (G3055) — a battle about words; rendered strifes of words.
Greek noseo (G3552) — to be sick, to dote; rendered doting, of a diseased craving for dispute.
Greek blasphemia (G988) — slander, reviling; rendered railings.
usage: “envy, strife, railings, evil surmisings” — the harvest of a quarrelsome man.
“proud, knowing nothing” — pride as the substitute for knowledge.
“from such withdraw thyself” — the apostolic counsel.

pos: n. pl. (contradictions; things set against; antitheses)
etymology: Greek antithesis, a setting against — the source of the English antithesis. The Authorized Version renders it oppositions, and the phrase it governs, science falsely so called, translates pseudonumos gnosis, knowledge under a false name.
biblical_def: O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called. This is the last charge of the letter, and it is a charge about custody. Timothy is not told to advance something but to keep it — to guard a deposit entrusted to him. Against that duty Paul sets two dangers. The first is profane and vain babblings, empty noise that consumes a ministry without nourishing anyone. The second is more formidable and is the reason the word oppositions matters: antitheseis, a system of contradictions, arguments arranged against the deposit. And Paul characterises the system exactly. It calls itself knowledge, and the name is false — science falsely so called, knowledge under an assumed name. The Authorized Version's science carries its older and wider sense of systematic knowledge, not the natural sciences. What Paul describes is any organised body of thought that claims the authority of knowledge in order to contradict revelation. His instruction is not to master and refute it but to guard what was committed and avoid the entanglement, and he tells Timothy why: which some professing have erred concerning the faith.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the act of opposing; that which is placed over against; contradiction; contrariety of position or opinion. SCIENCE, knowledge; the comprehension of truth or facts by the mind.
webster_full: OPPOSITION, n. Situation so as to front something else; a standing over against.
OPPOSITION, n. Contrariety of interests, measures or designs; contradiction; resistance.
SCIENCE, n. In a general sense, knowledge, or certain knowledge; the comprehension or understanding of truth or facts by the mind.
SCIENCE, n. In philosophy, a collection of the general principles or leading truths relating to any subject.
BABBLING, n. Foolish talk; senseless prattle; idle or unmeaning words.
scriptures: 1 Timothy 6:20
O Timothy, keep that which is committed to thy trust, avoiding profane and vain babblings, and oppositions of science falsely so called:
1 Timothy 6:21
Which some professing have erred concerning the faith. Grace be with thee. Amen.
Colossians 2:8
Beware lest any man spoil you through philosophy and vain deceit, after the tradition of men, after the rudiments of the world, and not after Christ.
1 Corinthians 3:19
For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. For it is written, He taketh the wise in their own craftiness.
corruption_summary: The verse is misread as a warning against natural science; Paul warns against any system that assumes the name of knowledge in order to contradict what God has revealed, and commands the guarding of the deposit rather than accommodation to it.
corruption_paragraphs: Because science now names the natural sciences almost exclusively, 1 Timothy 6:20 is quoted as though Paul had anticipated laboratories. He had not. Gnosis is knowledge in general, and Webster's 1828 entry still carries the older English breadth: knowledge, the comprehension of truth or facts by the mind. Paul's target is any organised body of claims that wears the name of knowledge falsely, and in his own century the incipient gnostic systems fit the description precisely. The dictionary has no quarrel with the study of God's works; it has a quarrel with systems that borrow the prestige of knowledge to contradict his word.

The live danger runs the other way. Each age produces a framework whose authority is thought settled, and theologians arrive to show that the faith can be restated in its terms — the documentary hypothesis reassigning Moses, the historical-critical method dissolving authorship and date, more recent frameworks recasting biblical anthropology in categories of power. Paul's charge is not to negotiate the deposit down to the terms of the reigning system but to keep it. He closes the letter by noting the cost of the alternative: which some professing have erred concerning the faith. The deposit is not the church's property to trade.
roots_summary: Greek antithesis (G477), a setting against; gnosis (G1108), knowledge; pseudonumos (G5581), falsely named; parakatatheke (G3872), a deposit committed in trust.
roots_lines: Greek antithesis (G477) — a placing against, a contradiction; rendered oppositions, its only occurrence.
Greek gnosis (G1108) — knowledge; rendered science in the older English breadth of the word.
Greek pseudonumos (G5581) — under a false name; rendered falsely so called, its only occurrence.
Greek parakatatheke (G3872) — a deposit entrusted for safekeeping; rendered that which is committed to thy trust.
Greek kenophonia (G2757) — empty sounding, vain babbling; the lesser of the two dangers named.
usage: “keep that which is committed to thy trust” — the charge is custody.
“science falsely so called” — knowledge under an assumed name.
“some professing have erred concerning the faith” — the cost, plainly stated.

pos: adj. (insolent; violently insulting; one who outrages others)
etymology: Greek hubristes, an insolent man — the noun behind the English hubris, meaning one who treats others with contemptuous violence for the pleasure of it. The Authorized Version's injurious carries the older English force of one who does injury, not merely one who is harmful.
biblical_def: Who was before a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and injurious: but I obtained mercy, because I did it ignorantly in unbelief. Paul is describing himself, and the three words mount. A blasphemer sins against God directly. A persecutor pursues God's people. Injurious is the strongest of the three and the least understood in modern English, because it now suggests something merely harmful. The Greek hubristes means an insolent man — one who inflicts outrage on others with contempt, who enjoys the humiliation he causes. Luke records the fact behind the word: Saul, yet breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord. Paul does not soften the self-description anywhere in his letters, and he returns to it as the measure of what he received: this is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief. The clause about ignorance is not an excuse, and it must not be read as one. Paul says he obtained mercy, which is precisely what a man with an excuse does not need; and he says he did it in unbelief, which names the ignorance as culpable. His point is that the mercy reached the worst case on record, so that no sinner after him may plead his own case is beyond it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): wrongful; unjust; hurtful; doing or occasioning injury; given to injuring others; contumelious.
webster_full: INJURIOUS, a. Wrongful; unjust; as an injurious proceeding.
INJURIOUS, a. Hurtful; mischievous; occasioning injury or damage.
INJURIOUS, a. Contumelious; reproachful; abusive; as injurious language.
BLASPHEMER, n. One who blasphemes; one who speaks of God in impious and irreverent terms.
PERSECUTOR, n. One that persecutes; one that harasses others with continued cruelty for adhering to a particular religion.
scriptures: 1 Timothy 1:13
Who was before a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and injurious: but I obtained mercy, because I did it ignorantly in unbelief.
1 Timothy 1:15
This is a faithful saying, and worthy of all acceptation, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners; of whom I am chief.
Acts 9:1
And Saul, yet breathing out threatenings and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord, went unto the high priest,
1 Timothy 1:12
And I thank Christ Jesus our Lord, who hath enabled me, for that he counted me faithful, putting me into the ministry;
corruption_summary: The clause about ignorance is regularly turned into a doctrine of diminished responsibility, and Paul's self-description into rhetorical humility; he means both literally, and the mercy is the greater for it.
corruption_paragraphs: Because I did it ignorantly in unbelief is pressed into service for a general principle that sin committed in ignorance is not properly guilt — a principle that would empty the doctrine of original sin and much of Romans 1, where men who did not like to retain God in their knowledge are without excuse. Paul is not pleading extenuation. He says in the same breath that he obtained mercy, and mercy is what is shown to the guilty. Unbelief is itself named as the condition of the ignorance, and unbelief is sin. What Paul offers is not a lighter verdict on his past but an explanation of why grace, and not justice, met him on the Damascus road.

A second and gentler distortion treats of whom I am chief as a pious overstatement — the sort of thing a humble man says. The present tense forbids it: not was chief but am. Paul, years into an apostolic ministry, still reckons himself the chief case, because he had been a hubristes, a man who outraged the saints with contempt. The doctrinal use he makes of it is exact and pastoral: if the worst was received, the pattern holds for all who come after. Reduce the self-description to modesty and the argument it was built to carry falls apart.
roots_summary: Greek hubristes (G5197), an insolent and violent man; blasphemos (G989), a blasphemer; diokes (G1376), a persecutor; eleeo (G1653), to obtain mercy.
roots_lines: Greek hubristes (G5197) — an insolent man who outrages others; rendered injurious, and elsewhere despiteful.
Greek blasphemos (G989) — a railer, a blasphemer; the first term of Paul's three.
Greek diokes (G1376) — a persecutor; its only occurrence, of Paul himself.
Greek eleeo (G1653) — to receive mercy; the verb that answers all three terms.
Greek agnoeo (G50) — to be ignorant; qualified here by in unbelief, which names it as culpable.
usage: “a blasphemer, and a persecutor, and injurious” — three terms, mounting.
“but I obtained mercy” — what the guilty receive.
“of whom I am chief” — present tense, years into the ministry.

pos: n. (want of self-restraint, especially in appetite)
etymology: Greek akrasia, from a-, not, and kratos, strength or mastery — want of self-mastery. The Latin incontinentia, from in-, not, and continere, to hold together or contain, gives the English exactly: a failure to hold oneself in.
biblical_def: Defraud ye not one the other, except it be with consent for a time, that ye may give yourselves to fasting and prayer; and come together again, that Satan tempt you not for your incontinency. Paul is giving practical direction to married Christians, and the direction is startlingly concrete. The marital relation is a debt owed, and to withhold it is to defraud — to deprive a spouse of what is due. Abstinence is permitted, but Paul fences it with three conditions: it must be by mutual consent, it must be for a time, and it must be for a stated purpose, fasting and prayer. Then the couple is to come together again, and the reason given is sober rather than romantic: that Satan tempt you not for your incontinency. The word names a real and expected weakness. Akrasia is want of self-mastery, and Paul assumes it in ordinary Christians rather than treating it as a mark of carnality. This is why he writes as he does throughout the chapter — to avoid fornication, let every man have his own wife, and let every woman have her own husband; and, if they cannot contain, let them marry: for it is better to marry than to burn. Marriage in Scripture is far more than a remedy for appetite, but Paul is not embarrassed to say that it is also that, and he gives the counsel as protection against a real adversary.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): want of restraint of the passions or appetites; indulgence of lust; free or illegal indulgence of sexual desire.
webster_full: INCONTINENCE, n. Want of restraint of the passions or appetites; indulgence of lust.
INCONTINENCY, n. The same as incontinence; want of self-restraint.
INCONTINENT, a. Not restraining the passions or appetites; unchaste.
DEFRAUD, v.t. To deprive of right, either by obtaining something by deception or artifice, or by taking something wrongfully without the knowledge or consent of the owner.
CONTAIN, v.i. To live in continence or chastity; to restrain the appetites.
scriptures: 1 Corinthians 7:5
Defraud ye not one the other, except it be with consent for a time, that ye may give yourselves to fasting and prayer; and come together again, that Satan tempt you not for your incontinency.
1 Corinthians 7:2
Nevertheless, to avoid fornication, let every man have his own wife, and let every woman have her own husband.
1 Corinthians 7:9
But if they cannot contain, let them marry: for it is better to marry than to burn.
1 Corinthians 7:7
For I would that all men were even as I myself. But every man hath his proper gift of God, one after this manner, and another after that.
corruption_summary: Two opposite errors meet on this text: an ascetic instinct that treats abstinence within marriage as the higher path, and a permissive one that denies the category of incontinency altogether.
corruption_paragraphs: The ascetic error is ancient and was already at work in Corinth, where some held it good for a man not to touch a woman and read celibacy as a superior grade of holiness. Medieval Rome institutionalised it, ranking the cloister above the household and imposing clerical celibacy the apostles did not impose. Paul's answer is to make the marital debt an obligation and prolonged abstinence the exception, permitted only by consent, only for a time, and only for prayer. He adds that every man hath his proper gift of God, which rules out treating either state as the higher calling. A spouse who withholds in the name of devotion is, in the apostle's word, defrauding.

The permissive error simply deletes the category. Where appetite is regarded as an identity to be expressed rather than a strength to be governed, incontinency ceases to name anything and becomes a word for prudishness. Scripture keeps the category and keeps it moral: akrasia is a want of self-mastery, and self-mastery is a fruit of the Spirit, listed as temperance. Paul's counsel is also practical in a way the modern account cannot match. He does not tell the tempted to suppress or to indulge; he tells a married couple to come together, and he names the adversary who is watching for the gap.
roots_summary: Greek akrasia (G192), want of self-mastery; apostereo (G650), to defraud or withhold; egkrateia (G1466), temperance or self-control; peirazo (G3985), to tempt.
roots_lines: Greek akrasia (G192) — want of self-mastery; rendered incontinency here and excess at Matthew 23:25.
Greek apostereo (G650) — to defraud, to keep back what is owed; rendered defraud.
Greek egkrateia (G1466) — self-mastery; rendered temperance, the fruit of the Spirit that answers akrasia.
Greek peirazo (G3985) — to tempt, to test; here the work of Satan in the opened gap.
Greek sumphonos (G4859) — agreeing together; rendered consent, one of Paul's three conditions.
usage: “that Satan tempt you not for your incontinency” — a real weakness, soberly assumed.
“Defraud ye not one the other” — the marital debt named as a debt.
“except it be with consent for a time” — the fenced exception.

pos: n. (leave granted; allowance as distinguished from command)
etymology: Greek suggnome, literally a thinking-with, a concession — agreement to allow rather than a requirement to obey. Latin permissio, from permittere, to let through, to let go.
biblical_def: But I speak this by permission, and not of commandment. Paul has just given his counsel about abstinence within marriage, and he pauses to mark the status of what he has said. The distinction is between a concession and a command. What he has allowed — a season of abstinence by mutual consent for prayer — is permitted, not required; a Christian couple who never take such a season have disobeyed nothing. The verse is therefore a small model of a large habit: the apostle is careful to tell his readers how binding each thing he says is. In the same chapter he distinguishes what he has from the Lord, what he says of himself, and what is concession, and he expects the church to weigh the difference. This is not uncertainty about his authority. Paul elsewhere writes with full apostolic weight and expects obedience. It is precision about the kind of thing being said, and it guards the conscience in both directions. Where God has commanded, no man may loosen; where God has permitted, no man may bind. Paul immediately adds the reason such matters cannot be legislated uniformly: every man hath his proper gift of God, one after this manner, and another after that.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the act of permitting or allowing; leave; license or liberty granted; allowance, as distinguished from command.
webster_full: PERMISSION, n. The act of permitting or allowing.
PERMISSION, n. Allowance; license or liberty granted; leave.
PERMIT, v.t. To allow; to grant leave or liberty to by express consent.
COMMANDMENT, n. A command; a mandate; an order or injunction given by authority.
CONCESSION, n. The act of granting or yielding, usually implying a demand, claim or request from the party to whom it is made.
scriptures: 1 Corinthians 7:6
But I speak this by permission, and not of commandment.
1 Corinthians 7:7
For I would that all men were even as I myself. But every man hath his proper gift of God, one after this manner, and another after that.
1 Corinthians 7:5
Defraud ye not one the other, except it be with consent for a time, that ye may give yourselves to fasting and prayer; and come together again, that Satan tempt you not for your incontinency.
1 Corinthians 7:2
Nevertheless, to avoid fornication, let every man have his own wife, and let every woman have her own husband.
corruption_summary: The verse is used to make Paul's teaching generally optional, as though he were offering opinions; he is doing the opposite, marking precisely which of his words bind and which do not.
corruption_paragraphs: A common use of 1 Corinthians 7:6 is to relativise apostolic teaching as such: if Paul concedes that he sometimes speaks by permission, then his instructions may be weighed as personal counsel wherever a reader finds them inconvenient. The inference runs backward. A writer who carefully labels one sentence as concession is telling you that the unlabelled sentences are not. Paul does exactly the same within this chapter, distinguishing what he has of the Lord from what he says himself, and the distinction only means anything because his ordinary word carries authority. Scripture is God-breathed throughout, and its own internal markers of command and concession are part of what is breathed out.

The opposite error binds where God has left free. A church that turns Paul's concession into a requirement — mandating seasons of abstinence, or ranking those who practise them — has done to this verse what Rome did to celibacy at large, and it burdens consciences God has not burdened. The doctrine of Christian liberty rests on the difference this verse marks. Where Scripture commands, the conscience is bound absolutely; where Scripture permits, no church, elder, or movement may bind it, and the attempt is itself a fault.
roots_summary: Greek suggnome (G4774), a concession or allowance; epitage (G2003), an injunction or command; charisma (G5486), a gift of grace.
roots_lines: Greek suggnome (G4774) — concession, allowance; rendered permission, its only occurrence.
Greek epitage (G2003) — an injunction, a command; the term Paul expressly denies of this counsel.
Greek charisma (G5486) — a gift of grace; rendered proper gift, the reason such matters differ between believers.
Greek epitasso (G2004) — to enjoin, to order; the verb behind commandment.
Greek eleutheria (G1657) — liberty; the doctrine that rests on the distinction this verse draws.
usage: “by permission, and not of commandment” — the status of the counsel, marked by the apostle.
“every man hath his proper gift of God” — why such matters are not legislated uniformly.
“except it be with consent for a time” — the concession itself.

etymology: Greek parallage, a change or variation — the word from which the English parallax descends, used of the shifting of a heavenly body's apparent position. James pairs it with shadow of turning, and both terms are drawn from the movement of lights across the sky.
biblical_def: Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning. The imagery is astronomical, and it is chosen with care. James calls God the Father of lights — the maker of sun, moon, and stars. Every one of those lights varies. The sun climbs and declines and casts a shadow that moves all day; the moon waxes and wanes; the stars wheel and set. Having named God as their Father, James then says the one thing that is not true of any of them: with him is no variableness, neither shadow of turning. The lights change; the One who made them does not. The doctrinal weight is the divine immutability, and James introduces it for an intensely practical reason. He has just warned that no man may say he is tempted of God, and he is establishing why the character of God can be relied upon absolutely: God does not have moods, phases, or a dark side that comes round in its season. What comes down from him is every good gift and every perfect gift, without exception and without alternation. The Scriptures say the same in plainer words: I am the LORD, I change not; and, God is not a man, that he should lie; and of the Son, Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): susceptibility of change; liableness or aptness to alter; changeableness; inconstancy.
webster_full: VARIABLENESS, n. Susceptibility of change; liableness or aptness to alter.
VARIABLENESS, n. Changeableness; inconstancy; instability; levity; fickleness.
VARIABLE, a. That may vary or alter; changeable; mutable; that may be altered.
IMMUTABLE, a. Unchangeable; unalterable; that cannot be altered or changed.
SHADOW, n. Shade within defined limits; obscurity or deprivation of light, apparent on a plane and representing the form of the body which intercepts the rays of light.
scriptures: James 1:17
Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, and cometh down from the Father of lights, with whom is no variableness, neither shadow of turning.
Malachi 3:6
For I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed.
Numbers 23:19
God is not a man, that he should lie; neither the son of man, that he should repent: hath he said, and shall he not do it? or hath he spoken, and shall he not make it good?
Hebrews 13:8
Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.
corruption_summary: Divine immutability is denied outright by process theology and qualified into insignificance by open theism; James asserts it as the ground of every good gift and of the believer's confidence in God's character.
corruption_paragraphs: Process theology denies divine immutability by construction, making God a being who develops with the world; open theism, following Pinnock, Boyd, and Sanders, denies exhaustive foreknowledge and so makes God a learner who adjusts as the future arrives. Both are errors, and both are answered here. James does not say God is reliable in the main, or unchanging in his essential character while variable in knowledge and purpose. He says no variableness and neither shadow of turning, using the language of celestial motion precisely in order to exclude even the slightest shift. Malachi grounds Israel's survival on the same fact: I am the LORD, I change not; therefore ye sons of Jacob are not consumed.

A common objection holds that immutability is a Greek philosophical intrusion, unable to account for the texts where God is said to repent. The Reformed answer is old and sound. Numbers 23:19 and 1 Samuel 15:29 state the doctrine flatly in the same canon that contains those texts, which means Scripture does not regard them as contradictory; the language of divine repentance describes God's unchanging purpose meeting changed creatures, not a change in God. Immutability is not divine coldness. It is the reason a believer's worst day does not find God in a different mood, and why what comes down from the Father of lights is good, and perfect, and does not alternate.
roots_summary: Greek parallage (G3883), variation or change; trope (G5157), a turning; aposkiasma (G644), a shadow cast; dosis (G1394), a giving or gift.
roots_lines: Greek parallage (G3883) — variation, the shifting of a light's position; rendered variableness, its only occurrence.
Greek trope (G5157) — a turning, as of the solstice; rendered turning, its only occurrence.
Greek aposkiasma (G644) — a shadow cast by something turning; rendered shadow, its only occurrence.
Greek dosis (G1394) — the act of giving, a gift; every one of them from above.
Hebrew shanah (H8138) — to change, to alter; denied of the LORD at Malachi 3:6.
usage: “with whom is no variableness” — immutability, stated of the Father of lights.
“neither shadow of turning” — no phase, no declining, no dark side.
“I am the LORD, I change not” — the same doctrine in the prophets.
